item.description: Friday evening edition — three sequence-based ML papers changing therapeutic development workflows. First, Feller/Secor/Swanson/Wilke/Deibler (Novo Nordisk Molecular AI + Wilke lab UT Austin; J Chem Inf Model DOI 10.1021/acs.jcim.6c00652, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.01.06.697994v3): PeptideCLM-2 — scaled-up SMILES chemical language model suite for therapeutic peptides. Pretraining corpus: 108,583,157 PubChem drug-like small molecules + 9,634,945 ESMAtlas peptides (filtered pTM>0.7, pLDDT>0.7, ≤100 aa) + 49,145 LIPID MAPS lipids; per-epoch balanced sampling (250K lipids upsampled + full 10M peptides + 10M downsampled small molecules) to prevent small-molecule collapse. Custom k-mer tokenizer max length 6, 405 tokens (160 single-atom + 245 k-mers), 64% sequence-length reduction on natural peptides vs atom-level SMILES. Architecture: BERT-style encoders + rotary positional embeddings + SwiGLU + pre-LN, 64-dim per attention head. Three scales: Small (6L, 384 hidden, 6H) = 32M params; Base (12L, 768, 12H) = 114M; Large (24L, 1024, 16H) = 337M. Three pretraining objectives: MLM only (span-masking rate 25%, Gaussian span length μ=3.5, σ=1.0), MTR only (regression to 99 RDKit descriptors), Hybrid (λ_MLM=0.6, λ_MTR=0.4). Nine models total (3 sizes × 3 objectives), all released. Optimization: AdamW (β1=0.9, β2=0.98, weight decay 0.01), 8×H100 GPUs, 3 pseudo-epochs, batch size 512, cosine LR schedule. Benchmarks vs prior baselines. Cyclic peptide membrane permeability (CycPeptMPDB) AUROC: best 0.836±0.011 (Hybrid); PeptideCLM-1 0.781; MoLFormer-XL below; Morgan fingerprints 0.792; RDKit99 descriptors 0.800. Tumor-homing peptide MCC (THPep): 0.756±0.019 (MLM-only) vs THPep published 0.710. Cell-penetration MCC (CellPPD): 0.875±0.004 (MLM-only) vs CellPPD-Mod 0.850. Antimicrobial peptide MCC (AmpHGT): 0.884±0.013 (MLM-only) vs AmpHGT 0.797; out-of-distribution generalization to noncanonical residues held out from AmpHGT training. Plasma stability MCC (PepMSND): 0.749±0.007 (MTR-only) vs PepMSND 0.726. Aggregation prediction (ThT fibrillation AUROC) scales monotonically with size: 32M=0.694, 114M=0.751, 337M=0.823 vs Morgan fingerprints 0.579 — showing large chemical LMs capture the subtle non-linear biophysical drivers of aggregation. Objective-size interaction: at 32M Hybrid beats MLM-only meaningfully; at 114M and 337M the gap closes, matching the general PLM scaling literature. Caveats: frozen embeddings give R²<0.30 on CycPeptMPDB regardless of size (linear probes unsuitable); benchmark data leakage <3.2% on most tasks but 8.06% on CycPeptMPDB and 28.43% on PepMSND. Code github.com/AaronFeller/PeptideCLM-2; weights on HuggingFace under aaronfeller/peptideclm-2; pretraining data Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.17993164; license CC-BY 4.0 (commercial reuse permitted). Practical implication: stronger peptide-chemistry feature extractor for peptide-drug conjugates, macrocyclic peptide antibody alternatives, and peptide-linker bispecifics; drop in behind PeptiVerse's SMILES branch for materially better developability prediction. Second, Schwarz/Giese/Gupta/Dziubańska-Kusibab/Villalba/Cherniack/Yang/Root/Karsli-Uzunbas/Greulich/Siegel/Kamburov (Bayer AG Machine Learning Research Berlin + Bayer R&D Oncology + Broad Institute + Owkin France; J Chem Inf Model DOI 10.1021/acs.jcim.6c00768): "Protein Language Model-Based Fitness Estimates Facilitate Resistance Mutation Identification." Problem: on-target amino acid mutations conferring drug resistance are a program-killing failure mode for kinase inhibitors; identifying them pre-clinical saves patient cycles and enables parallel follow-up compound development. Free-energy perturbation (FEP) affinity estimates for single-residue mutations is the workhorse, but produces false positives — mutations FEP flags as affinity-decreasing may also destroy protein function (non-folded, non-active), so they can't emerge as resistance in vivo despite the reduced binding. Filtering non-viable mutants with physics stacks (stability + activity modeling) is expensive and error-prone. Method: combine FEP affinity estimates with protein-language-model fitness (masked-LM likelihood as viable-protein proxy). Low PLM likelihood → mutation not in natural sequence space → filter out (natural selection has already run the "is this a viable protein" experiment). Validation: two DMS datasets testing single-site resistance to a known inhibitor with known binding mode. Public Broad Institute DMS on ERK2 tested against SCH772984 inhibitor. Internal Bayer DMS on EGFR exon 20 mutant tested against a Bayer small-molecule inhibitor. Finding: PLM fitness filter reclassifies FEP false positives correctly — FEP-flagged affinity-decreasing mutations with low PLM likelihood are DMS-non-resistant (filtered out), while FEP-flagged mutations with high PLM likelihood are DMS-resistant (retained). Effectively replaces expensive stability/activity simulation with a cheap sequence-model likelihood. Caveats: on-target resistance only (off-target compensation, PK escape out of scope); per-site single-mutation validation only, no combinatorial escape tested; specific PLM choice underspecified in abstract. Antibody-audience relevance: antibody escape is the structurally-mirrored problem — FEP on antibody-antigen interface filtered by antigen fitness = the same recipe applied to bnAb escape prediction against variable antigens (HIV Env, influenza HA, SARS-CoV-2 spike, oncogenic drivers). Open question the recipe raises: general PLM (ESM) vs pathogen-specific fitness model conditioned on the actual antigenic landscape. Third, Marescal/Cheeseman (Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research + MIT Department of Biology; bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.16.739020, posted 2026-07-17): "A machine learning model predicts protein stability of annotated and alternate protein isoforms." Multi-layer perceptron regressor trained on Timms et al. dataset (~50,000 peptide sequences × Protein Stability Index scores 1-6 from Global Protein Stability GPS assay: GFP fluorescence readout for GFP fused to candidate N-terminal 23-residue peptide, quantifying stability effect). One-hot encoding, 80/20 random train/test split. Test R²=0.72, train R²=0.97. Permutation-based interpretability: for each of top-500 stable sequences, generate all single-amino-acid substitutions, identify significant destabilizations. Position 1 accounts for 95% of significant destabilizations, ranked destabilizers matching Arg/N-end rule: Tyr, Lys, Arg, Trp, Asp, Phe, His, Asn, Leu, Gln, Glu, Ile (primary type-1 + type-2 + secondary + tertiary degrons). Stabilizing substitutions at position 1: Ser, Ala, Met, Thr, Pro, Gly, Val — small side chains, matching biological literature. Reverse permutation (top 500 unstable → stabilizing substitutions): 37% of significant stabilizations arise from positions 3-23, not the first two. Confirmed by training a 2-residue-only model: R² 0.37 train / 0.36 test — dramatically worse than full 23-residue model. Novel finding: Arg or Lys substitutions at positions 4-13 (deeper than classical N-end rule) increase predicted stability. Experimental validation via reporter constructs: start with two most unstable N-termini in dataset (ADAM10 PSI=1.49, ZNF208 PSI=1.41), generate 6 modified peptides each with progressively more arginines at positions 6-11, measure GFP stability via GPS system. Model predictions and experiments agree — monotonic stabilization with increasing Arg content. Mechanism dissection: for ADAM10 VLI at positions 5-7, mutate to DDD, AAA, TTT, or RRR. All four stabilize (loss of hydrophobic effect), but RRR stabilizes more than DDD/AAA/TTT — disentangling loss-of-hydrophobic-residue from gain-of-arginine — establishes a genuinely new sequence rule beyond the classical N-end rule. Application: predict stability across alternative-start-site N-terminal protein isoforms (thousands catalogued via translation-initiation-site profiling — some upstream extensions, some downstream truncations, all in-frame). Model identifies isoform pairs where the extension/truncation of a few residues predicts dramatically different stability from the annotated version. Relevance for antibody engineers: N-terminal composition can be intentionally tuned for antibody or antibody-fusion stability; the model scores candidate designs and surfaces the arginine-positional rule as a design lever beyond the standard first-two-residue N-end reasoning.

item.title: Night: Scripps Research PNAS — MPER HIV-1 broadly neutralizing antibody structural anatomy: groove-mediated (DH511/10E8) vs heavy-chain-mediated (4E10/PGZL1/VRC42) lipid recognition, cardiolipin polyreactivity tied to somatic maturation stage in DH511 lineage, PGZL1 CDR H3 anionic patch limits nonspecific lipid contacts, sequential prime-boost immunogen design strategy targeting groove-mediated engagement; SweetFold (bioRxiv) — glycan-aware Boltz-1x adaptation representing glycans as pseudo-polymers with explicit anomeric state and glycosidic connectivity, improved structural metrics across monosaccharide/oligosaccharide/lectin/glycoprotein benchmarks; biological continued pretraining of 26B MoE model (Gemma-4-26B-A4B) on 8.7B tokens DNA+protein+biomedical text lifts MMLU +13 pts, MBPP nearly 2×, BixBench MCC 0.23→0.92 without catastrophic forgetting; subsequent SFT narrows all axes back to near-base, revealing CPT and SFT as complementary not substitutable stages
item.description: Friday night edition — three items. First, Cho/Rantalainen/Ozorowski/Lu/Tingle/Lee/Ward/Schief/Wilson (Scripps Research Institute + IAVI, PNAS DOI 10.1073/pnas.2609827123, published 2026-07-14): structural basis of membrane engagement and polyreactivity control in HIV-1 MPER broadly neutralizing antibodies. MPER broadly neutralizing antibodies (DH511, 10E8, 4E10, PGZL1, VRC42) all contact viral membrane lipids during recognition, creating an autoreactivity tolerance barrier. Paper determines crystal structures of DH511.1 (memory B cell-derived), DH511.12P (plasma cell-derived), and VRC42.01 in complex with MPER peptide and phosphatidic acid, plus cryo-EM of DH511.2 bound to membrane-embedded Env. Integrative analysis with prior MPER bnAb structures yields two mechanistic bins. Groove-mediated binders (10E8, DH511): shape-complementary lipid engagement through deep grooves, positively charged residues adjacent to but not directly contacting lipid headgroups; DH511 builds an aromatic cage from CDR H3 + light chain and approaches the membrane at a distinct tilt angle vs 10E8; DH511.12P carries tyrosine substitutions at specific CDR H3 positions that enhance coordination of viral envelope lipids while suppressing host membrane binding — differential cardiolipin polyreactivity tied to somatic maturation stage. Heavy-chain-mediated binders (4E10, PGZL1, VRC42): direct hydrogen bonds to lipid headgroups via positively charged CDR H1 patches; 4E10 has strongest positive patch, highest polyreactivity; VRC42.01 has weaker positive patch, lower polyreactivity; PGZL1 adds CDR H3-mediated negative patch creating electrostatic repulsion with negatively charged lipid headgroups. Design grammar: reduce CDR H1 positive-charge density or introduce anionic CDR H3 counterbalance for heavy-chain-mediated binders; tune CDR H3 tyrosine composition for groove-mediated binders. Sequential immunization logic: prime with germline-targeting immunogens clearing early autoreactivity checkpoint, boost with membrane-anchored Env driving somatic hypermutation toward groove-mediated engagement using topologically constrained membrane immunogens (favor engagement with virus membrane in narrow fusion-exposure window while limiting access to flat host membranes). No ML component — structural biology + structural reasoning — but directly informs computational immunogen design, antibody-membrane interaction models, and polyreactivity prediction training data annotation. Full text accessed via Jina proxy from PNAS. Second, Sundar/Yang (bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.16.738959, posted 2026-07-17): SweetFold — glycan-aware adaptation of Boltz-1x for structure prediction of free glycans, glycoproteins, and protein-glycan complexes. Abstract-only (body not yet rendered, posted today). Key design: glycans represented as pseudo-polymers rather than generic ligands, preserving monosaccharide identity, anomeric state, glycosidic connectivity, and atom-level stereochemistry; paired with glycan-specific architecture changes, stereochemical supervision during training, and sugar-centric training curriculum. Evaluated across monosaccharide, oligosaccharide, lectin-glycan complex, and glycoprotein benchmarks: improved structural metrics relative to Boltz-1x baseline without regression on protein-only benchmarks. Relevance: glycan shields on major antibody targets (influenza HA, HIV Env, coronavirus spike) create neutralization epitope geometry problems; improved glycoprotein structure prediction propagates into epitope accessibility, antibody-antigen docking pipeline accuracy, and glycoform-specific immunogen design; also relevant to Fc glycosylation modeling for effector-function-optimized antibodies. Third, Wang (bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.06.736700, posted 2026-07-16): biological continued pretraining reshapes foundation model capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Re-analysis of three checkpoints from a single 26B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts lineage (Gemma-4-26B-A4B): instruction-tuned base, same model after biological CPT on 8.7B tokens of DNA + protein sequence + biomedical text, and after subsequent supervised fine-tuning on the CPT checkpoint. Results across three capability axes — general knowledge/reasoning (MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag), code generation (MBPP), biomedical knowledge (BixBench). Biological CPT lifts rather than degrading: MMLU +13 pts, MBPP pass@1 doubles (0.33 → 0.63), BixBench MCC 0.23 → 0.92. Single regression: TruthfulQA -8.8 pts (interpretable domain drift, not general degradation). Vocabulary expansion control ablation: <0.4 pt on every general metric, so gains attributable to CPT not tokenizer changes. Subsequent SFT narrows all three axes back to near-base levels. Interpretation: CPT re-organizes and lifts the shared capability substrate; SFT cashes it out onto target tasks at the cost of general breadth. Training-order implication for antibody language model practitioners: biological CPT first, task-specific SFT second; both stages are complementary not substitutable; collapsing into a single SFT or reversing the order leaves general-capability gains on the table. Abstract-only (body not rendered).

item.description: Friday briefing — three items, none exclusive to antibodies but all directly informative for antibody-model builders. First, Würtzen/Mamica/Kanduri/Pavlović/Greiff/Peters/Sandve (Greiff lab at Oslo, Peters lab at La Jolla Institute for Immunology, Sandve lab at Oslo; bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.10.737788, posted 2026-07-16): "What Do Generative Models Learn About Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoires? A Benchmark Study." Motivation: standard ML metrics — held-out likelihood, perplexity, nearest-neighbor distance — do not cleanly translate to AIRR sequence data because the repertoire is shaped by V(D)J recombination and thymic/peripheral selection, and there is no biological ground truth for "in-distribution" receptor. Consequently, the field has selected models on home-cooked evaluations. This paper applies a suite of AIRR-tailored metrics against five model families: variational autoencoders, long short-term memory recurrent networks, antibody language models, explicit selection models (in the Elhanati/Mora tradition of separating generation and selection stages), and statistical baselines. Task framed on individual-specific immune receptor repertoire modeling — clinically relevant for personalized immunotherapy, disease monitoring, and vaccine-response studies where the pan-population distribution is not the right prediction target. From the abstract the axes probed are memorization risk (how much of a generated repertoire is training-set copies with cosmetic edits), innovation capability (how much is genuinely novel receptor space consistent with biology), and hyperparameter sensitivity. Detail-limited caveat: preprint went up yesterday and bioRxiv has not rendered the full body HTML yet; specific model rankings, per-metric numbers, and the code release are not yet extractable. The design and framing themselves are worth flagging — a shared benchmark with tailored metrics from the group that has been arguing longest that generic ML evaluation misreads immune data is scaffolding the field is overdue for. Second, Zhang/Wei/Zheng et al. (J Chromatogr A DOI 10.1016/j.chroma.2026.467271, published 2026-07-16): leveraging protein language model for maturation of high-affinity peptide ligand for AAV vector purification. Application-side problem: AAV downstream affinity purification currently uses immobilized-antibody resins requiring harsh low-pH elution that stresses the capsid and reduces recovery; peptide ligands offer mild elution but nanomolar-comparable affinity is hard to reach without directed evolution. This paper targets the receptor-binding region on the AAV2 capsid, uses a de novo design method to nominate 3 candidate peptide ligands, then routes them through ESM3-guided maturation over 3 rounds of docking simulations. Output: peptide A4 with Kd = 3.8 μM for AAV2; MD analysis attributes binding to electrostatic interactions. Resin: A4 coupled to Sepharose 4 Fast Flow (Sep4FF-A4) shows good selectivity and serotype specificity for AAV2, effective adsorption at pH 6-8, mild elution. Not a spectacular affinity number in isolation (the Menegatti group's 2023 peptides sit in the same range), but methodologically noteworthy — a protein language model drives maturation of a de novo peptide against a non-antibody target to usable purification performance in 3 rounds without a directed-evolution wet campaign. Open question the abstract leaves: how much of the win comes from ESM3 versus the closed-loop design in general; a companion study running the same loop with AbMPNN or ProteinMPNN would isolate that. Third, Zhang/Chatterjee (Chatterjee lab, Duke; bioRxiv 10.64898/2025.12.31.697180 → Nat Commun DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-74167-w, published 2026-07-16): PeptiVerse — a unified platform for therapeutic peptide property prediction. Backbones: ESM-2 at the 650M-parameter scale (esm2_t33_650M_UR50D) for amino-acid input, PeptideCLM-23M-all for SMILES input covering chemically modified peptides (non-natural amino acids, backbone modifications, macrocycles). Architecture: frozen foundation embeddings + task-specific lightweight heads (XGBoost, Elastic Net, SVM, MLP, CNN, Transformer, selected per property); binding-affinity task uses a cross multi-head attention transformer over peptide-and-protein embeddings for a joint latent representation. Property coverage: hemolysis (both modalities), non-fouling (both), solubility (AA-only), permeability-penetrance (AA-only), permeability-PAMPA/Caco-2 (SMILES-only), toxicity (SMILES-only), half-life (both), binding affinity (both). Benchmarks (Spearman ρ or F1) vs PepLand: amino-acid binding affinity 0.557 vs 0.503; SMILES permeability 0.671 vs 0.628; permeability-penetrance F1 0.929 vs 0.838; solubility F1 0.754 vs 0.662; one honest loss on SMILES binding affinity (0.582 vs 0.768) where PepLand's number is under random splits with train-test similarity leakage while PeptiVerse's is under similarity-aware splits — the honest number is the meaningful one. No wet-lab validation of predictions in the paper. Web interface at Hugging Face Spaces (ChatterjeeLab/PeptiVerse), weights on Hugging Face, plotting code on GitHub. Utility: developability filter for chemically modified peptide or macrocycle campaigns, closes the loop on a generative design workflow that produces candidates upstream; especially relevant for cyclic peptide antibody-alternative work in T-cell engagers and similar formats.

item.title: Night: HELM-BERT (Okuno lab, Kyoto U, J Chem Inf Model 2026) — DeBERTa-based encoder-only peptide language model pretrained on 39,079 HELM-notated therapeutic peptides (linear + cyclic); scaffold-split cyclic-peptide membrane-permeability R²=0.668 retains best mean performance vs SMILES baselines (MoLFormer-XL, PeptideCLM), architecture-matched SMILES control narrows gap under full fine-tuning but HELM-BERT keeps advantage under frozen-representation linear probing, arguing monomer- and topology-explicit notation is more data-efficient than atom-level SMILES for chemically modified peptides; competitive PPI prediction on Propedia + ChEMBL; code (github.com/clinfo/HELM-BERT) + weights (HF Flansma/helm-bert) released. PeptideSGCL (Shandong U / Macao Polytechnic, ACS Synth Biol 2026) — multimodal peptide-property predictor pairing ProtBERT sequence encoder with hierarchical GNN-Transformer structural encoder + parallel graph-spatial-channel attention; inter-intra hybrid supervised contrastive learning combines cross-modal alignment with intramodal class-supervised separation; outperforms baselines on hemolysis + non-fouling prediction tasks — transferable recipe for antibody-CDR developability classifiers pairing antibody LMs (AbLang/IgLM) with structural encoders over IgFold/ABodyBuilder predictions
item.description: Thursday night edition — two smaller peer-reviewed peptide-language-model papers indexed on PubMed within the last day. First, Lee/Koyama/Maeda/Matsumoto/Okuno (Kyoto U Graduate School of Medicine, J Chem Inf Model, DOI 10.1021/acs.jcim.6c00451; arXiv preprint 2512.23175 posted 2025-12-29): HELM-BERT, the first encoder-based peptide LM trained on HELM (Hierarchical Editing Language for Macromolecules) notation. Motivation: for therapeutic-peptide chemistry, atom-level SMILES obscures cyclic topology and monomer boundaries, while amino-acid-level protein LMs cannot encode noncanonical residues or explicit cross-links — HELM keeps monomer identity as tokens and connectivity as an explicit connection statement, so the model does not have to reconstruct residue/ring topology from atoms. Architecture: DeBERTa (disentangled attention over content + position vectors, enhanced mask decoder, n-gram-induced encoding) — good match for HELM's dual-signal structure (position of monomer in primary sequence + identity in large monomer vocab). Pretraining: 39,079 chemically diverse peptides (linear + cyclic). Downstream: (1) cyclic-peptide membrane permeability — random-split R² = 0.668; retains best mean performance under Murcko scaffold split (a harder generalization test that forces disjoint core scaffolds between train and test), outperforming SMILES-based baselines MoLFormer-XL and PeptideCLM. Architecture-matched SMILES control narrows the gap under full fine-tuning but HELM-BERT keeps a clearer advantage under frozen-representation linear probes — the pretrained embedding geometry is what does the work, and it survives without task-specific fine-tuning. (2) Peptide-protein interaction prediction on Propedia + ChEMBL benchmarks — competitive with protein-LM baselines on natural-amino-acid peptides, HELM-BERT keeps its advantage on modified peptides. Embedding analysis: HELM-BERT preserves macrocyclic topology in a linearly accessible form (simple linear probes recover ring size / cross-links from frozen embeddings). Ablation isolates disentangled attention as the critical DeBERTa component for HELM. Code: github.com/clinfo/HELM-BERT; weights: HF Flansma/helm-bert. Caveat: 39k-peptide corpus is small vs protein-LM foundation scale — HELM-BERT is a modality-specific encoder for chemically modified peptides, not a general protein LM replacement. Transferable design pattern for the antibody-conjugate audience: representation-notation choice matters more than parameter count when your modality is data-poor and vocabulary-rich; pretraining a modestly-sized encoder on a notation that keeps structural constraints explicit outperforms much-larger encoders trained on obscuring notations. Second, Cai/Xiong/.../Wei (Shandong U + Macao Polytechnic + Tianjin U, ACS Synth Biol, DOI 10.1021/acssynbio.6c00318): PeptideSGCL, a multimodal dual-contrastive framework for peptide property prediction. Sequence encoder: ProtBERT (250M-param protein LM trained on UniRef100). Structure encoder: hierarchical GNN-Transformer stack (local topology via GNN layers + long-range dependencies via transformer layers) + parallel graph spatial channel attention module. Contrastive objective: inter-intra hybrid supervised contrastive loss — combines cross-modal (sequence↔structure) alignment with intramodal class-supervised contrast (same-class peptides pulled together, different-class pushed apart, in each modality). Downstream: hemolysis + non-fouling binary classifications; overall performance superior to baseline models. No wet-lab validation (method paper). Why notice it: recipe generalizes directly to antibody CDR-loop developability classifiers pairing antibody LMs (AbLang/IgLM) with structural embeddings from IgFold/ABodyBuilder predictions; dual-contrastive setup is a reasonable default when the downstream task is a discrete developability call (soluble vs aggregation-prone, expressible vs not).

item.title: Afternoon: Nozach group (Paris-Saclay) DMS + Deep Learning engineering of cross-reactive anti-PD-L1 antibody C4 — CNN ensemble trained on 63,000 DMS-labeled sequences from three FACS gates classifies affinity; minimal-mutation enumeration finds 4-5 substitution variants (DL.1) matching the 13-15-substitution DMS variants at sub-nanomolar KD for both human and mouse PD-L1, 95.9% humanness vs 86-89% for DMS variants, CT26 syngeneic tumor survival matching Avelumab (bioRxiv); Sahtoe/Knowles de novo protein binders for the alpha-synuclein NAC beta-strand — 30,000 RFdiffusion backbones filtered to 21 designs, 3 in vitro + in-cell hits, one round of partial diffusion matures strongest binder from 238 nM to 1.94 nM (120×), NMR confirms designed antiparallel beta-sheet fold, strict selectivity vs tau/amylin/amyloid-beta, kinetic dissection reveals distinct microscopic-step inhibition per binder — strongest (17_2) preferentially engages on-pathway oligomers and inhibits secondary nucleation at 10% substoichiometric ratio (Hubrecht/Cambridge, bioRxiv)
item.description: Thursday afternoon edition — two items squarely in the antibody + protein-design lane. First, Dorison/Grindel/.../Nozach (CEA/Paris-Saclay, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.15.738714, posted 2026-07-16): ML-guided engineering of cross-reactive antibodies with minimal mutations. Starting molecule C4 — fully human anti-PD-L1 with nM binding to human PD-L1 and only 200-300 nM binding to mouse PD-L1 — the species barrier that blocks preclinical evaluation in immunocompetent mouse models. Pipeline: (1) yeast-display Fab DMS with FACS sorts for improved mouse-PD-L1 binding while preserving human-PD-L1 binding, generating multi-layer heatmaps identifying ~20 hotspot positions in CDRH1/H2/H3 and FWK3; (2) combinatorial library at hotspots sorted at progressively lower mouse-PD-L1 concentrations produces 10 first-generation cross-reactive IgG variants (DMS.1-10) with sub-nM to low-nM KD for both orthologs but 13-15 substitutions per clone; (3) three-way classifier trained on FACS-sorted deep-sequencing labels (17k/20k/26k unique sequences in parental/enhanced/strongly-enhanced gates) — RF, XGBoost, and ConvNeXt-style CNN compared. CNN chosen for full-sequence input (captures serendipitous mutations outside designed positions), ensemble of 3 models on downsampled subsets, test accuracy 87.5-92% on three-way problem. Instead of generative design: enumerated all 120,000 sub-mutation-set variants of the 10 DMS clones (removing substitutions one at a time and combinatorially), classified with CNN ensemble at >80% confidence agreement across models; 9 sequences meet unanimous ++ prediction at minimum of 4 substitutions. DL variants tested by BLI: KD matches DMS variants (sub-nM to low-nM); FACS on CT26 mouse cells shows EC50 0.23-0.58 nM (DL) vs 0.18-1.02 nM (DMS); humanness 95.9% for 4-sub, 94.9% for 5-sub vs 86-89% for DMS variants. Antigen DMS mapping of the functional epitope shows both DL.1 (4 mutations) and DMS.1 (15 mutations) preserve the C4 epitope centered on the PD-1 binding site; AlphaFold3+Protenix+IntelliFold co-folding converges (iRMSD 0.88 Å), buried R50-C4/E41-hPDL1 salt bridge central to interface; N59F substitution rationalized by loss of R96-hPDL1 replacement with C95-mPDL1 (hydrophobic vs polar). CT26 syngeneic colorectal tumor in immunocompetent mice, 5 IV dose groups of 10 each: median survival 26 and 30.5 days for DMS.1 and DL.1 vs 11-18.5 days for parental C4 and isotype control, matching Avelumab. Payoff: DMS + FACS-gated CNN classifier + exhaustive minimal-mutation enumeration = interpretable extraction of mutational couplings (L55V and G56P interchangeable but at least one required; N59F essential; A33G and S31R roles distinguishable). Second, Zhang/Han/Ortigosa-Pascual/.../Sahtoe/Knowles (Cambridge/Hubrecht, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.13.738012, posted 2026-07-14): potent substoichiometric inhibition of alpha-synuclein aggregation by de novo oligomer-binding proteins. Target: NAC domain (residues 61-95) of alpha-synuclein — intrinsically disordered in monomer, adopts extended beta-strand in fibrils; drives Parkinson-disease aggregation. Pipeline: ~30k RFdiffusion backbones targeting the NAC beta-strand → 1,954 after DSSP/SASA filter → 91 after ColabFold → 21 after manual interface inspection → 3 in vitro + in-cell hits (DFASYN008/013/017). Initial KDs 238 nM to 3.78 μM. One round of partial diffusion (noise-then-redenoise) affinity maturation: 8_4 → 416 nM (~1.5×), 13_9 → 410 nM (~9×), 17_2 → 1.94 nM (~120×). NMR titrations (2D 1H-15N HSQC/HMQC on 15N-labeled binders + unlabeled αSyn peptide) confirm binding-induced ordering; TALOS-N secondary structure indices on assigned 8_4/αSyn complex match design; NH-NH NOEs confirm designed antiparallel β-sheet. Selectivity by BLI vs tau/amylin/Aβ: 17_2 strictly selective (no binding at concentrations tested); 8_4 3-20× selective; 13_9 non-selective (open-faced hydrophobic surface) — architecture, not sequence, determines discrimination. HeLa fluorescent recruitment assay (membrane-anchored NAC-mScarlet + EGFP-binder under dox control): Pearson 0.57 (8_4), 0.77 (13_9), 0.90 (17_2) tracking in vitro affinities. Multi-state affinity profiling (Fluidity One-M + custom smMDS): 8_4 monomer/oligomer/fibril = 1.54/2.20/23.13 μM; 13_9 = 405 nM/2.78 μM/401 nM; 17_2 = 304 nM/126 nM/500 nM — 17_2 preferentially engages oligomer species (most closely linked to toxicity). Thioflavin-T aggregation kinetics at 10% substoichiometric binder-to-monomer ratio: all three completely block fibril formation for 180-h assay. Seeded aggregation at varying seed concentration to separate primary nucleation, secondary nucleation, and elongation: 8_4 and 13_9 inhibit elongation + secondary nucleation; 17_2 inhibits secondary nucleation almost exclusively (spares elongation) by sequestering on-pathway oligomers. Transferable lesson: partial diffusion as trivial-cost single-round affinity maturation can move 100×; state-resolved binding + kinetic dissection of microscopic aggregation steps is the characterization model for design campaigns against multi-state functional targets.

item.title: Baker lab generative transmembrane beta-barrel nanopores via TMB_RFD2 + TMB_MPNN fine-tuning on 117k AlphaFold-curated structures — 60-80% E. coli expression, crystal structures within 0.73-1.15 Å RMSD, selective ion sensing + DNA translocation + polymer-membrane transport demonstrated (Baker lab, bioRxiv v2); KaMLESM — ESM2/ESMC protein language models achieve near-experimental-precision pKa prediction from sequence alone; ESM Cambrian outperforms ESM2-15B at all sizes, uniform layer-depth improvement argues architecture and training data quality matter more than parameter count (Jana Shen lab, bioRxiv v3)
item.description: Thursday briefing — two items, a lighter day. Philomin/Coventry/Bera/Baker et al. (Baker lab, University of Washington, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.06.04.729630 v2, posted 2026-07-15): generative AI design of programmable asymmetric transmembrane beta-barrel nanopores. Core problem: TMBs have structural constraints (glycine twists, beta-bulges, membrane-specific amino-acid composition) that existing RFdiffusion + ProteinMPNN cannot handle. Two-part solution: (1) TMB_RFD2 — RFdiffusion2 fine-tuned on 117,447 TMB structures distilled from AlphaFold2 predictions of 485,000 TMB sequences (orders of magnitude more than the ~700 PDB TMBs), with 1D conditioning on glycine-twist and beta-bulge placement. (2) TMB_MPNN — ProteinMPNN with expanded 96-nearest-neighbor receptive field (vs default 32) retrained on the same distillation set for TMB-appropriate amino-acid composition. Results: 60-80% E. coli expression on TMB_RFD2 + TMB_MPNN designs (vs 0% for off-the-shelf ProteinMPNN on any backbone). 48 designs across 10/12/14/16-stranded barrels characterized; electrophysiology shows stable pore conductances at 0.7-1.5 nm diameter range. Crystal structures of N10_RS_des4 (Ca RMSD 1.15 Å) and N10_AP_des7 with specified glycine twists (Ca RMSD 0.726 Å) confirm atomic-level design accuracy. Functional demonstrations: copper-binding lumen for selective ion sensing (overriding Irving-Williams selectivity series), 14-stranded pores supporting DNA translocation, long pores with increased hydrophobic thickness for transport across 3D networks of monoglyceride bilayers and synthetic polymer-lipid hybrid membranes. Transferable recipe for antibody engineers: build structural-class-specific distillation datasets from AlphaFold predictions, condition the backbone generator on class-specific structural features, expand the sequence designer receptive field to cover the full interface — same strategy would apply to CDR-loop-optimized RFdiffusion fine-tuning on an OAS-derived CDR distillation set. Shen/Dayhoff/Kortzak/Shen (Jana Shen lab, University of Maryland, bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.04.17.649309 v3, posted 2026-07-15): KaML-ESM — predicting protein pKa values from sequence alone using ESM2 and ESMC (ESM Cambrian) embeddings fed to a multilayer perceptron. Pretraining on synthetic pKa dataset from structure-based KaML-CBTree model; fine-tuned on PKAD-3 (1,167 experimental pKa values in 247 proteins). Separate acid/base models for mechanistically distinct residue classes. KaML-ESM2 (layer 31 embeddings from ESM2-650M): RMSE near experimental precision limit ~0.5 pH units for Asp, Glu, His, Lys. v3 adds KaML-ESMC (final layer 80 from ESMC-6B, trained on 2.78B sequences): consistently lower RMSE than ESM2 at all sizes including ESM2-15B. Layer analysis: ESM2 shows non-monotonic layer-accuracy pattern with amino-acid-specific optima (overall best at layer 31); ESMC shows monotonically decreasing error toward final layer, suggesting capacity not yet saturated. Interpretation: ESMC architectural improvements and training diversity, not raw parameter count, drive the electrostatic representation advantage. Antibody-engineering relevance: sequence-based pKa prediction enables early-stage screening for charge-state-related developability liabilities (aggregation propensity, high-concentration viscosity, pH-dependent solubility) before structural characterization; ESMC as preferred feature extractor for charge-sensitive tasks.

item.title: Evening bonus: GB-0669 — first-in-human Phase 1 of a Generate Biomedicines AI-designed half-life-extended monoclonal antibody targeting the conserved SARS-CoV-2 spike S2 stem helix, 51 healthy adults, dose-proportional PK to 2400 mg, 54-day half-life, dose-dependent live-virus neutralization at 600/1200 mg, mild AEs only (J Infect Dis); Hou et al. — protein language model scaling is non-monotonic for fitness prediction: ESM2/MSA-Transformer/EVE/ESM-IF1/ESM3 across 154 ProteinGym experiments show performance peaks at moderate p(wildtype) and collapses when large models push p(wildtype) into an extreme regime where all mutation likelihoods become uninformatively uniform (Shen lab, Columbia, Nat Comput Sci); Koohy/Deane labs — 100× accelerated AlphaFold 3 pipeline for TCR:pMHC benchmarked on IMMREP25 shows AF3 binding scores are dominated by TCR-over-pMHC positioning rather than interface chemistry; a PAE Aggregator ML head refines scores enough to cluster sequence-similar TCRs by binding mode and recapitulate mutational scanning (Oxford, bioRxiv v3)
item.description: Wednesday evening bonus edition — three items on what AI-designed antibodies do in humans, why bigger protein language models are not always better for fitness prediction, and what AlphaFold 3 actually contributes to T-cell specificity prediction. First, Borriello/Koh/Troconiz/Nassirpour/Goyal et al. (Generate Biomedicines, J Infect Dis DOI 10.1093/infdis/jiag349, published 2026-07-14): first-in-human trial of GB-0669, a half-life-extended monoclonal antibody optimized using Generate's AI design platform and targeting the conserved S2 stem helix of the SARS-CoV-2 spike (an epitope with less selection pressure than the RBD). Preclinical safety in cynomolgus monkeys, then Phase 1 in 51 healthy adults 18-55 across five ascending single-IV cohorts (100, 300, 600, 1200, 2400 mg) with 43-week follow-up. All AEs mild (grade 1 or 2), no dose-limiting toxicities. Dose-proportional PK up to 2400 mg, terminal half-life 54 days (consistent with proper Fc engineering, comparable to nirsevimab). Dose-dependent serum live-virus neutralization at 600 and 1200 mg with separation from placebo; author-defined neutralizing index (serum concentration × in vitro potency) supports therapeutic coverage for ~2 weeks post-single-dose. In vitro combination testing with remdesivir/nirmatrelvir/molnupiravir shows improved neutralization profile. Proposed Phase 2 at 1200 mg for immunocompromised COVID-19 patients. Framing: this is the first-in-class fully-computationally-optimized commercial antibody to reach human safety readout, and it does not exhibit the hidden polyreactivity or PK weirdness that would falsify the AI-antibody design premise. Second, Hou/Liu/Zafar/Shen (Yufeng Shen lab, Columbia University, Nat Comput Sci DOI 10.1038/s43588-026-01010-z, published 2026-07-13; preprint 10.1101/2025.04.25.650688 v4): protein language models estimate p(sequence), which reflects the fitness landscape and is used for zero-shot mutation effect prediction. Widely believed in DL: bigger = better. This paper shows for fitness prediction it isn't. Across 154 ProteinGym experiments, models tested include ESM2 (all sizes), MSA-Transformer, EVE, ESM-IF1, ESM3. Performance is best in a moderate p(wildtype) regime; at very high p(wildtype) models predict uniformly high likelihoods for essentially all substitutions (nothing looks implausible relative to a well-memorized reference), and at very low p(wildtype) predict uniformly low likelihoods — both extremes collapse into uninformative noise. Larger models tend to push p(wildtype) higher, so scaling up moves many proteins above the moderate-p sweet spot and degrades fitness prediction, even though the larger model is objectively a better generative prior over natural sequences. Practical guideline: pick the model whose p(wildtype) sits in the moderate range for the target sequence, not the largest available model. Antibody-engineer implication: mid-sized antibody LMs (AntiBERTa/AbLang/IgLM in the ~100M-few×100M range) may already be in the right regime for CDR-scoring tasks; naive scaling to billions of parameters could be counterproductive. Third, McMaster/Elmoselhy/Ilievski/Thorpe/La Gruta/Rossjohn/Deane/Koohy (Hashem Koohy lab, University of Oxford, with Charlotte Deane and Jamie Rossjohn, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.08.737208 v3, posted 2026-07-15): characterising AlphaFold 3's ability to predict T-cell antigen specificity. item.description: Wednesday afternoon bonus edition — four items, thread is antibody escape and de novo binder generalization. First, Kikawa/Bloom et al. (Fred Hutch Cancer Center, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.02.18.706711 v2, posted 2026-07-14): "Near real-time data on the human neutralizing antibody landscape to influenza virus as of early 2026 to inform vaccine-strain selection." Barcoded pseudovirus sequencing-based neutralization assay: library of 53 recently circulating H3N2 + 30 recently circulating H1N1 hemagglutinins + 8 past vaccine strains = 91 HAs × 186 barcoded variants; panel of 302 human sera (ages 0-103, five geographic sites, mostly Oct-Nov 2025); 27,409 titers total. H3N2: median titers vary >3-fold across strains; subclade K (derived from J.2.4 with HA1 mutations K2N/S144N/N158D/I160K/Q173R/T328A) has significantly lower titers than all other current subclades; subvariants adding mutations in antigenic regions D (sites 96, 207, 223) and E (site 261) drop titers further. H1N1: subclade D.3.1.1 (from D.3.1 with R113K/A139D/E283K/K302E) has lower titers than parent D.3.1 and current NH vaccine strain. Age-stratified pattern in H1N1: adolescents and young adults have much lower titers to H1N1 strains with mutations at sites 155 or 157. Post-vaccination titer increases modest (~1.5-2.5× for H3N2, smaller for K and other newest subclades; regionD-mutated K variants get only ~1.5×) — data publicly available with Nextstrain integration for real-time vaccine-strain informed decisions. Second, Simonich/McMahon/Juviler/Bloom et al. (Fred Hutch, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.02.12.705519 v2, posted 2026-07-14): "Complete definition of how antibodies used to prevent RSV are affected by F mutations." v2 adds DMS for candidate antibodies 1A2 and 1B6, DMS against five human polyclonal sera, and expanded validation neutralization assays. Two pieces: (1) biophysical model — when Fab affinity is high, bivalent IgG binding buffers mutations that reduce Fab affinity; when Fab affinity is moderate, buffering vanishes. Nirsevimab has higher Fab affinity for RSV-A than RSV-B → escape mutations that look silent against RSV-A show measurable IgG neutralization loss against RSV-B. Validated with K68Q and (K/N)201S mutations. Implication: measure escape in Fab form for cross-strain generalizability. (2) Pseudovirus deep mutational scanning of near-all F-ectodomain point mutations in the subtype-A Long strain, measuring cell-entry fitness + neutralization by nirsevimab, clesrovimab, suptavumab, RSM01, 1A2, 1B6 (IgG + Fab) + 5 polyclonal human sera. New clesrovimab-escape sites identified: 426, 429, 433, 470 (beyond known 443, 445, 446). New nirsevimab escape substitutions beyond known 64-73/201-216 landscape. Escape scores validated against natural high-escape-score RSV strains; sporadic natural resistance seen but no sustained spread. Polyclonal sera: no single mutation reduces serum neutralization by more than a few-fold; mutations that do modestly affect sera cluster at F apex near nirsevimab epitope. Nextstrain-integrated escape trees for surveillance. Third, Zhang/Ke/Zhi/Jin/Cao et al. (Longxing Cao lab, Westlake University, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.13.738243, posted 2026-07-14): physics-based generative de novo design of small-molecule and metal-ion binders using ProBuilder — Rotamer Interaction Field (RIF) enumerates energetically favorable side-chain-ligand contacts, backbone construction anchored at RIF residues via Monte Carlo fragment assembly with joint RPX folding score + RIF binding score, sequences designed with Rosetta + ProteinMPNN + AlphaFold2 self-consistency filtering. Small-molecule results (helical bundles, mostly 120 aa, 5-6 helices): dolutegravir 14/96 designs bound, best 4.94 μM → 971 nM after helix-extension optimization; cianidanol 20/94; DFHBI 2/16; serotonin 6/38, best 72.8 μM → 29.9 μM after four rounds of sequence optimization; dopamine 1/33 at 75.0 μM (single binder — hardest target). Interface-disrupting mutations abolish binding, confirming designed pockets. Metals: 65-aa four-helix bundles designed to be metastable in absence of metal, folded on binding. Zinc binder ZK2: 150 nM KD, tetrahedral coordination, 1:1 stoichiometry, no binding to Cu²⁺/Co²⁺/Ni²⁺ (overrides Irving-Williams series). Nickel binder NiM4: 5.38 μM, octahedral, high selectivity. Crystal structures: serotonin-bound SRO_30 (2.58 Å, Cα RMSD 0.97 Å to design), dopamine-bound DPA_9 (2.47 Å, Cα RMSD 0.79 Å), zinc-bound ZK2 (1.23 Å, Cα RMSD 0.45 Å). Biosensor engineering: split-cpsfGFP serotonin sensor wcSRO30_1.0 with ΔF/F₀ 339.9%, EC50 539.9 μM, size 129 aa vs iSeroSnFR 272 aa; split-cpsfGFP dopamine sensor at ΔF/F₀ 37.5% (first reported soluble de novo dopamine biosensor); split-NanoLuc zinc sensor with EC50 ~73 nM and strong Zn selectivity. Fourth, Marsalkova/Simecek (CEITEC/Masaryk University, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.05.07.723606 v2, posted 2026-07-14): "Advancing Knotted Protein Design with ESM3: Guided Generation and Topological Insights." ESM3-SM (1.4B params, fp16 on A10G) with derivative-free guided decoding + Topoly Alexander-polynomial knot scoring achieves 89% (95% CI 81-94%) knotted-topology success from fully masked sequences, vs ~0.5% for unguided diffusion. Trefoil (3₁) most common in generated set (33/70 resolved); complex topologies up to 9 crossings produced. Generated knots have lower ESM3 pLDDT (0.32) / pTM (0.21) than real knots evaluated in the same pipeline (0.90 / 0.84) — treat as topology-enriched samples pending independent validation. Robustness on real knotted proteins: 84% sequence must be altered before knot breaks, sharp threshold not gradual; at 50% masking RMSD already 3.24 Å but knot probability 0.85; topology encoded distributively across sequence, decoupled from specific 3D arrangement. MLP on frozen mean-pooled ESM3 embeddings hits 97.1% knot classification accuracy. Generated proteins <15% sequence identity to any known knot (mean 11.6%, indistinguishable from random baseline), arguing against memorization. Transferable lesson for antibody-LM practitioners: guided decoding with a task-specific scorer as a lightweight steering primitive without fine-tuning, and evidence that general protein-LM embeddings encode distributed global features robustly enough for probing.

item.description: Wednesday morning briefing — five items, thematically about pushing more of the antibody-engineering pipeline into learned representations or automated closed loops. First, Salaris/Pinter/Cioppi et al. (ETH Zurich, Patterns DOI 10.1016/j.patter.2026.101561, published 2026-07-10): H3BERTa — a RoBERTa-architecture transformer with ~86M parameters trained on ~18M CDR-H3 sequences from the Observed Antibody Space (OAS) database (IgG + IgA from healthy unvaccinated donors), MLM objective, 113 epochs, final loss 1.58. Head-to-head with AntiBERTa2 (pretrained on full heavy variable regions). UMAP: H3BERTa clusters primarily by J-gene (IGHJ segments contribute CDR-H3 C-terminus), AntiBERTa2 primarily by V-gene (accesses framework). Both models yield strongly bimodal LDA separation of naive vs memory B cells and support antigen-binding discrimination on immunized alpaca sequences (SARS-CoV-2 spike, human IL-6, human TNF-α) with comparable separability. HIV-1 bnAb classifier: linear-kernel SVM on frozen H3BERTa embeddings against a 390-CDR-H3 labeled set (bnAbs from CATNAP + hard negatives from OAS) achieves 93% test accuracy, macro-F1 0.92; GAN-H3BERTa semi-supervised variant yields more structured latent space with similar classification. Applied blind to a full HIV-1 donor bcr repertoire, both classifiers correctly place the experimentally validated bnAb and two other neutralizers in high-confidence bnAb regions. Repertoire-level PPL analysis on ~4.4M healthy + ~4.2M bnAb-donor sequences (Roskin et al.): central PPL distribution overlaps, but tails differ statistically — healthy repertoires higher PPL in upper tail, opposite direction in lower tail; low-PPL sequences enriched in tyrosine and longer loops (consistent with affinity-matured contacts), high-PPL sequences shorter and leucine-rich. Practical take: scope of input matters as much as parameter count for repertoire tasks; H3BERTa is species-agnostic (CDR-H3 is least species-specific) and enables full-repertoire-scale mining at fraction of the compute of full-variable-region models. Second, Wang/Jin/Pan (Ainnocence, Inc., bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.13.738250, posted 2026-07-14; competing interest — commercial model): frozen protein foundation-model embeddings for antibody-antigen ΔΔG ranking. Affinity maturation cast as learning-to-rank over point mutations. Under identical 5-fold CV, a regularized linear probe on frozen AINN-P1 (autoregressive protein foundation model) embeddings already exceeds a from-scratch task-specific end-to-end baseline; an optimized lightweight head raises mean Spearman rank correlation from 0.42 to 0.53 (~28% relative), trains in seconds without any foundation-model fine-tuning. Interpretation: linear probe beating end-to-end model implies the gain is representation quality, not downstream capacity. Frozen Spearman 0.53 is moderate, not strong — framed as lower bound expected to be exceeded by task-adaptive fine-tuning. Third, "Automation and Active Learning for the Multi-Objective Optimization of Antibody Formulations" (Advanced Science DOI 10.1002/advs.76551, published 2026-07-13): closed-loop DBTL pipeline for GRAS-restricted excipient formulation. ML predictor of formulation behavior trained on multi-objective outputs (melting temperature as stability proxy, translational diffusivity, high-concentration viscosity). Automation-assisted formulation produces dozens of unique compositions on demand; results feed back into next round of model-designed experiments. Pipeline converges on both improved formulations and accurate predictive models across objectives; models map underlying property-function landscape (not just point-optimize). Operationalizes developability as an active-learning problem. Fourth, Kendell/McShinsky/Modzelewska et al./Gambles (U Utah, Commun Biol DOI 10.1038/s42003-026-10602-4, published 2026-07-13; MATCH IP pending): MATCH — modular split-antibody T-cell engager platform assembling multi-specific engagers over CD19/CD20/CD38 for B-cell malignancies. COMPASS — computational framework integrating T-cell counts, tumor burden, antigen expression to predict individualized multi-specific therapy compositions maximizing tumor kill while preserving T-cell viability (T-cell exhaustion treated as hard cost). Validation: (1) COMPASS predictions match effective formulations on CLL patient PBMC; (2) COMPASS-predicted compositions produced significantly improved survival in human lymphoma xenograft mouse model. Lab-in-the-loop: patient measurement → prediction → per-patient composition. Antibody-engineer implication: bispecific/multispecific design value shifts from finding the single best construct to producing composable specificities the framework can mix at point of care. Fifth, Zhang/Han/Ortigosa-Pascual et al. (Sahtoe + Knowles groups, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.13.738012, posted 2026-07-14): potent substoichiometric inhibition of alpha-synuclein aggregation by de novo oligomer-binding proteins. Target: intrinsically disordered NAC domain of α-synuclein, which lacks stable epitope but preferentially adopts extended β-strand upon assembly engagement — binders designed to present matching β-strand recognition scaffold and stabilise that conformer. Deep-learning-based protein design → 21 expressed → 3 engage target in vitro and in live cells. One round of partial diffusion (partial noise + re-denoise conditioning on target) as affinity-maturation step; best binder KD 1.94 nM, no detectable cross-reactivity to tau/amylin/amyloid-β. Solution NMR confirms peptide association and conformational changes consistent with intended architecture. Kinetic modeling with seeded-aggregation experiments + monomer/oligomer/fibril affinities resolves the specific microscopic step each binder inhibits: most potent binder selectively captures on-pathway oligomers (species most tied to neurotoxicity) and suppresses fibril formation at substoichiometric ratios without engaging bulk monomer pool. Transferable lesson: partial diffusion works as an affinity-maturation operator — no full redesign cycle needed to go from functional-but-modest to nanomolar, parallels the RFantibody-family workflow for antibody CDR maturation.

item.title: Night: ESM3 geometric atlas — modality fusion between layers 25–35 with sequence joining last after layer 28; functional annotation permanently orthogonal; structural disorder delays fusion (Steenwyk, bioRxiv); Schneidman-Duhovny lab review of deep learning for adaptive immune receptor structure prediction and design — AIR-specific LMs, inverse folding, diffusion backbone generation, sequence-space diffusion, challenges in CDR-loop modeling and epitope-specific design (Hebrew University, Curr Opin Struct Biol)
item.description: Night edition — two items. First, Steenwyk (Life Sciences Research Foundation / Vanderbilt, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.08.737319, posted 2026-07-12): "A geometric atlas of how ESM3 organizes modalities across depth." Representational-similarity analysis applied to ESM3-sm-open-v1 (1.4B parameters, 48 transformer layers) once per modality in isolation across all 48 layers; 5,555 proteins from 12 organisms spanning bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes. The five input modalities are: amino-acid sequence, 3D structure, SS8 (8-state secondary structure), SASA (solvent accessibility), and functional annotations. Key findings: (1) Four physical modalities (sequence, structure, SS8, SASA) begin in distinct subspaces, remain maximally separated through ~layer 25, then fuse into a shared low-dimensional subspace between layers 25–35. Fusion is ordered — structure-derived modalities (structure, SS8, SASA) are mutually aligned from the input and fuse with each other first; sequence joins last, after layer 28. (2) Functional annotation never fuses: remains representationally orthogonal to physical modalities at every layer, whether annotation is whole-protein or per-residue — content-driven, not tokenization artifact. (3) Fusion is a learned property: absent in a randomly-initialized model of the same architecture. (4) Fusion reorganizes variance: between-condition variance converts to within-condition variance while the stream never approaches isotropy. (5) Fusion depth is independent of protein length but delayed by structural disorder. (6) Universal: all 12 organisms across all superkingdoms peak at the same network depth (layer 35). Practical implications: adapter insertion before layer 28 preserves the pre-fusion sequence representation; the 25–35 band is richest for structural probing; functional-annotation orthogonality means annotation tokens do not corrupt physical-property representations; disordered regions (including CDR loops) fuse modalities later than framework residues, a mechanistic account of why CDR modeling is harder. Second, Cohen/Hochner/Schneidman-Duhovny (Hebrew University, Curr Opin Struct Biol DOI 10.1016/j.sbi.2026.103326, published 2026-07-10): review of deep-learning progress for adaptive immune receptors (antibodies + TCRs). Covers AIR-specific language models, structure prediction, epitope-conditioned design. Generative strategies reviewed: inverse folding, diffusion-based backbone generation, sequence-space diffusion, sequence-structure co-design. Datasets and evaluation metrics discussed with explicit sources of bias and need for improved benchmarks. Challenges enumerated: flexible CDR-loop modeling, reliable AIR-antigen complex ranking, scalable epitope-specific AIR design. Full text paywalled; abstract-only summary here.

item.title: Evening: GB-0669 — first-in-human Phase 1 of an AI-designed monoclonal antibody targeting SARS-CoV-2 spike S2 stem helix (Generate Biomedicines, J Infect Dis) — n=51, 100–2400 mg IV ascending doses, 54-day half-life, dose-dependent serum live-virus neutralization at 600/1200 mg with 2-week neutralizing-index window, no DLTs; Nat Comput Sci mechanistic account of why bigger protein language models degrade at fitness prediction — model performance depends on how well p(sequence) matches evolutionary patterns, with a moderate-likelihood sweet spot; larger models push wildtype p(sequence) past the sweet spot into a compressed high-end where mutation rankings degenerate (Shen lab, Columbia); PeptideCLM-2 — SMILES-based chemical language model suite trained on >100M molecules for therapeutic-peptide native representation, beats prior methods on membrane diffusion, biological function, and half-life prediction (Novo Nordisk Molecular AI + UT Austin, J Chem Inf Model); MDMI — two-stage structure-guided peptide-design pipeline from tiny labeled datasets, structure-aware predictor + genetic algorithm cuts an all-negative false-positive rate from 70% to near zero and yields 4× more in-silico binders than baselines; split-GFP wet-lab testbed hits 38% sequence divergence with function retained in stage 1 and >50% in stage 2 (Pardee lab, U Toronto, bioRxiv)

Half-life-extended Fc. Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled first-in-human: n=51 healthy adults 18–55, five ascending IV doses (100/300/600/1200/2400 mg), 36 GB-0669 / 15 placebo, 43-week follow-up. Pre-clinical safety in cynomolgus monkeys clean. No DLTs; all AEs grade 1 or 2. Dose-proportional PK to 2400 mg, half-life 54 days. Dose-dependent serum live-virus neutralization at 600 and 1200 mg with clear placebo separation; neutralizing index (concentration × in-vitro potency) supports therapeutic-level activity for ~2 weeks post-dose. Combination in-vitro with remdesivir, nirmatrelvir, molnupiravir shows improved neutralization profiles. Supports Phase-2 at 1200 mg in immunocompromised patients. Paper does not detail the internal AI design pipeline (proprietary Generate platform integrating sequence/structure/developability), but this is the first published clinical readout for an antibody carrying the AI-designed label — the "developability/in-vivo PK wall" prediction against generative antibody design is now falsified on at least one molecule. Phase-2 efficacy remains to be shown. Second, Hou/Liu/Zafar/Shen (Columbia University Irving Medical Center, Systems Biology + Biomedical Informatics + Sulzberger Genome Center + Program for Mathematical Genomics, Nat Comput Sci DOI 10.1038/s43588-026-01010-z, published 2026-07-13): "Understanding language model scaling for protein fitness prediction." Mechanistic account of the well-known but under-explained anomaly that protein-LM fitness-prediction performance peaks at intermediate model size and declines beyond it. Zero-shot mutation-effect prediction uses model-assigned p(sequence) as fitness proxy, with mutant/wildtype likelihood ratio for ranking. Authors show model size, training-set composition, and stochastic training bias predicted p(sequence) away from real fitness. Performance depends on how well p(sequence) matches evolutionary patterns in homologs — best achieved at a moderate p(sequence) level. At extreme predicted wildtype likelihoods, models emit uniformly low or high likelihoods for nearly all mutations and ranking degenerates. Larger models tend to assign higher p(sequence) to observed sequences (sharper natural-distribution modeling), pushing many proteins past the moderate sweet spot into the compressed high-end — the mechanism by which scale hurts fitness prediction. Practical implication: check wildtype p(sequence) under the model before assuming bigger is better; consider ensembling across sizes; motivates antibody-specific LMs whose training distribution places antibody wildtypes in the moderate-likelihood band. Companion "Perspective" piece by Wang (Tsinghua) frames the same argument. Third, Feller/Secor/Swanson/Wilke/Deibler (Novo Nordisk Molecular AI + UT Austin Integrative Biology, J Chem Inf Model DOI 10.1021/acs.jcim.6c00652, published 2026-07-13): PeptideCLM-2 — a suite of SMILES-based chemical language models trained on >100M molecules with curated peptide-scale sequences, targeting the modality gap between protein LMs (restricted to canonical amino acids) and small-molecule chemical LMs (choke on polymer-length peptides). Native representation of non-canonical amino acids, N-methylation, cyclization, D-amino acids, non-peptide moieties. Benchmarks on three therapeutic-peptide endpoints (membrane diffusion, biological function, half-life) beat prior methods including static chemical descriptors and custom multi-embedding pipelines. Antibody-relevance: technology-transfer path toward SMILES-scale models for ADCs (antibody-payload-linker triples) and low-data-regime developability prediction. Fourth, Bayat/Perkins/Pardee (University of Toronto, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.13.737974, posted 2026-07-14, body not yet rendered — abstract-only): MDMI — Minimal Data Maximal Insight — two-stage structure-guided pipeline for functional peptide variants from tiny (tens-to-hundreds) annotated datasets. Stage 1 uses ML predictor on 3D structural features from predicted peptide-protein complexes (interface geometry + binding energetics) paired with a genetic algorithm. Structure-aware featurization cuts false-positive rate from 70% (sequence-only baseline) to near zero on an all-negative benchmark and produces ~4× more high-confidence in-silico binders than SOTA peptide/protein-design baselines. Wet-lab testbed uses split-GFP fluorescence readout for peptide-protein complementation: Stage 1 hits up to 38% sequence divergence from wildtype with retained activity; Stage 2 motif-guided recombination of Stage 1 successes reaches >50% divergence and reveals two functional clusters in sequence space. Full-length GFP fusion of a top candidate retains GFP-like emission, supporting fluorescent-scaffold formation. Transferable pattern for antibody CDR redesign — small labeled datasets, need diverse alternatives retaining same-epitope binding — where "predicted peptide-protein complex" swaps to "predicted antibody-antigen complex" and split-GFP swaps to an affinity assay.

item.title: TEDlm — domain-centric protein language model beats ESM-2-3B on CATH S40 remote homology at 650M params (AUROC1 0.28 vs 0.22); TEDlm3D with distance-guided contact loss reaches 0.50, matching Foldseek from sequence alone (Jones lab, UCL, bioRxiv); de novo conformation-selective miniprotein modulators of focal adhesion kinase — 33/96 designs modulate activity, low-nM inhibitors and 2×+ activators, cross-kinase redesign to Src (Baker lab, bioRxiv); AlphaFold3 audit across 5 application areas — uneven performance, training-set-adjacency dependence, model confidence fails on protein-RNA (Beltrao lab, U Fribourg/Lausanne, bioRxiv); ESM3-SM guided decoding + Topoly Alexander-polynomial scoring hits 89% knotted-protein success vs 0.5% unguided diffusion, 84% sequence perturbation before knot breaks (bioRxiv); asymmetric structural transfer — language-to-biology transfer strengthens with scale (drop 0.08), biology-to-language decays toward chance (drop 0.36), replicated across ESM-2 and ProtBERT (bioRxiv)
item.description: Monday morning briefing — five items, all posted 2026-07-13 or 2026-07-14, strong methodological day. First, Wei/Kandathil/Buchan/Jones (UCL, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.09.737428, posted 2026-07-13): TEDlm — masked language model pre-trained on structurally-defined domain segments from The Encyclopedia of Domains rather than full-length UniRef sequences. Standard MLM objective; TEDlm3D variant adds a distance-guided contact loss supervising attention maps against Cα–Cα geometry during pre-training. On CATH S40 remote-homology (<40% identity), 650M TEDlm scores AUROC1 0.28 at final layer vs ESM-2 3B at 0.22 — domain-centric pretraining beats 5× parameter scale-up. TEDlm3D reaches 0.50, approaching Foldseek's structure-based 0.53 from sequence at inference. Contact signal is in the encoder itself: attention-map probes and categorical Jacobian recover contact structure, not just a trained head. Zero-shot Molecular Function prediction substantially better than ESM-2; biophysical property tasks (dominated by local composition) comparable. Direct implication for antibody-LM builders: antibody variable domains are exactly one TED domain, argues restricted-domain pretraining (AntiBERTy, AbLang, IgLM) was correct choice; TEDlm3D contact loss transfers cleanly to paired-structure pretraining with SAbDab/AF3-multimer/IgFold coordinates. Second, Bauer/Lee et al./Baker (UW IPD + collaborators, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.10.737808, posted 2026-07-13, body not yet rendered — abstract-only): de novo genetically encoded miniprotein binders targeting focal adhesion kinase (FAK) with conformation-selective framing — each design targeted to stabilize a specific FAK conformational state (active vs inactive). 96 designs → 33 modulate kinase activity (~34% hit rate consistent with modern RFdiffusion+ProteinMPNN+AF filter pipelines). Top 4 characterized: 2 inhibitors with low-nM IC50s, 2 activators (>2× activity potentiation). Modulators preserve in-vitro directional effects in cells. Cross-kinase transfer: FAK inhibitors redesigned computationally to target Src kinase work — platform-level result. Design pipeline not spelled out in abstract but authorship + framing implies standard RFdiffusion + ProteinMPNN + AF-filter stack; novelty is conformation-selective scaffolding and demonstration that both inhibition and activation are accessible from the same platform. Complements antibody engineering — intracellular targets are outside the antibody-accessible space. Third, Follonier/Liu et al./Beltrao (U Fribourg + U Lausanne, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.13.738147, posted 2026-07-13, body not yet rendered — abstract-only): audit of AlphaFold3 across five application areas — ubiquitinated protein structure, TCR–peptide-MHC recognition, antibody-antigen complexes, protein-RNA, protein-lipid. Headline: AF3's extension to new biomolecule types shows less consistent performance and generalisation than AF2's monomer/multimer gains. Accuracy in several tasks depends on presence of related complexes in the training set (memorization/adjacency effect). Specific critical finding: in protein-RNA predictions, model confidence fails to separate genuine from decoy interaction partners — confidence metric untrustworthy for RNA-target screening. Antibody-antigen task included; specific number pending body render but consistent with "good in favourable settings, dependent on training-set overlap, less broadly generalisable than AF2" — matches anecdotal experience with novel epitopes and unusual CDR H3 / germline usage. Practical frame: AF3 is powerful for hypothesis generation and prioritisation but confidence metrics must be used with awareness of training-set overlap on an application-by-application basis. Fourth, "Advancing Knotted Protein Design with ESM3" (bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.05.07.723606, posted 2026-07-14): ESM3-SM (1.4B params, smallest open-source variant, fp16 on NVIDIA A10G via Modal) with derivative-free guided decoding using Topoly Alexander-polynomial scoring (30 random-projection stochastic closures per evaluation) to design knotted proteins. Guided ESM3 achieves 89% success (95% CI 81–94%) vs ~0.5% for unguided diffusion (RFdiffusion, EvoDiff) — dramatic gap but explicitly guided-vs-unguided not architecture-matched. Robustness: 84% of sequence must be perturbed on average before knot breaks; loss follows sharp threshold not gradual degradation; structural drift (RMSD) accumulates well before topology fails — topology more robust than specific 3D arrangement in ESM3 representation. Generated knot types include trefoil (33), figure-eight (10), torus 5₂ (10), plus 8₁₉, 9₄₄, 9₄₅. No close sequence similarity to known knotted proteins (KnotProt/AlphaKnot 2.0) — not memorization. Practical for structurally unusual antibody scaffolds — cyclic-permuted VHHs, disulphide-constrained topologies. Fifth, "Asymmetric Structural Transfer Between Natural Language and Biological Foundation Models" (bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.09.737502, posted 2026-07-13, abstract only): reverse-transfer study asking whether protein LMs fine-tuned on English structural tasks acquire zero-shot linguistic competence, in the same way English-fine-tuned LMs had been shown to acquire zero-shot protein-homology discrimination. Answer: reverse transfer is consistently weak, does not exceed matched-token controls, does not scale, does not generalize. Architecture-matched 2×2 with known training data (eliminates pretraining-contamination confound): language→biology off-domain drop 0.08 vs biology→language 0.36. Scaling widens the gap — language-to-biology strengthens with size, biology-to-language decays toward chance. Replicated across ESM-2 and ProtBERT families. Implication: initializing specialized biological models from general-purpose LMs is asymmetrically favoured over the reverse; "biological sequences are just another language" fails in operationally symmetric sense.

item.title: Night: BCR-Mistral — 500M-parameter decoder-only DNA BCR language model beats ESM-2-650M and Ab-RoBERTa on MS-associated repertoire embedding across 11.5M IGH sequences (Krishnan/Macklin, U Colorado Anschutz, bioRxiv); RFdiffusion+ProteinMPNN motif-scaffolding of N-Myc TAD yields single-digit-nM Aurora-A miniprotein inhibitors with crystal-structure-verified αG-helix + activation-loop convergent signature (Bayliss lab, Leeds, bioRxiv); Blood Transcriptional Module aggregation beats gene-level features by 14–25 AUC points on pan-vaccine (influenza/HepB/YF) high-responder prediction across 1,032 participants (Tomic/Przytycki, Boston U, bioRxiv)
item.description: Monday night supplement — three items, all posted 2026-07-13. First, Peet/Krishnan/Macklin (University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.07.735316): BCR-Mistral — nucleotide-level decoder-only DNA foundation model for BCR IGH sequences, downscaled from Mistral-7B architecture; three variants at 100M/300M/500M parameters, 500M model kept. Trained on ~2M heterogeneous OPIG OAS IGH sequences selected by iterative random sampling in 7-mer Euclidean space; nucleotide-level tokenization, random rotation, up to two 20-nt attention masks, up to one-third length truncation as augmentation; AdamW, effective batch 2400, 8 AMD MI100 GPUs. Outperforms ESM-2-650M and Ab-RoBERTa on same-disease-different-patient embedding triplet distances and cosine similarity; protein-tokenized variant of same architecture on same corpus performs worse than DNA variant, arguing nucleotide tokens capture codon-bias / silent-mutation signal beyond protein level. Downstream: 3-layer MLP classifier (256/128/64) on last-token embeddings for 5-way disease classification (healthy / autoimmune / infectious / other / MS); custom "dynamic exclusion" loss progressively drops MS sequences confidently classified as non-MS from the loss (analogous to semi-hard example mining), raising held-out precision. Study-grouped (not patient-grouped) CV folds surface study-driven artifacts. Data foundation: exhaustive NCBI SRA reanalysis of "multiple sclerosis" runs (December 2024 snapshot) with manual metadata curation + TRUST4 assembly + OPIG OAS = 11.5M IGH sequences from ~800 patients, 2.8M with full VDJ. Patient-level: 128-waypoint fixed-D repertoire embedding via joint reconstruction+contrastive optimization in hidden-state space; XGBoost on waypoint + sequence-classification inputs; ROC AUC >0.8 for MS vs healthy/infectious, lower for MS vs other autoimmune. Validation: correctly ranks 3/4 known PLP1c-binding myelin-specific IgGs above isotype control; longitudinal fingolimod/natalizumab treatment reduces disease-associated repertoire fraction (n small, not individually significant but direction consistent). Confirmed antibody binding to O4+ oligodendrocytes by flow. Code (upon publication) at github.com/krishnanlab/bcr-mistral-final; weights + processed data at Zenodo 20432913. Second, Miles/Bayliss (University of Leeds + University of Oxford Gergely lab, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.12.737516): RFdiffusion motif-scaffolding of N-Myc TAD residues 73–84 (short) and 73–89 (long) with Aurora-A hotspots, ~3,893 backbones across two motif sets, ProteinMPNN 1–2 seqs/backbone, AF2-initial-guess filter (iPAE<10, pLDDT>84, 2.5–3% hit rate); 17 designs selected. 15 express in E. coli, 8 inhibit Aurora-A ADP-Glo with fittable IC50s. Top designs DBS1 (IC50 12 nM, KD 0.9 nM by ITC — sub-nanomolar), DBS5 (IC50 16 nM), DBL5 (IC50 31 nM, KD 3 nM). ~1000× affinity gain over parent N-Myc peptide (KD ~12 μM). 9 crystal structures at 1.79–2.9 Å reveal convergent design signature — extensive αG-helix engagement via C-terminal helix + hydrogen bond / main-chain contact to activation loop; weak binders have shorter/bent C-terminal helices. DBL5 H55A mutation removes activation-loop H-bond → 10× IC50 loss to 425 nM, causally confirms the pattern. Aurora-B selectivity: DBS1 retains weak Aurora-B activity (100× less than Aurora-A), other selective binders essentially inactive on Aurora-B in ADP-Glo. Kinase-structure basis for selectivity: M233→L289 in P+1 pocket + non-conserved αG-helix residues Y334/Q335 in Aurora-A vs Aurora-B/C. Cellular: HeLa GFP-fusion transfections reduce Aurora-A T288 autophosphorylation at spindle poles for DBL5 and DBS1; DBS1 (only) also modestly reduces Histone H3 pS10; IP-MS: DBL5/DBS2/DBS5 pull down only Aurora-A + TPX2 as common interactors (24–42 proteins each), DBS1 promiscuous (215 interactors including MARK2, MELK). AF3 ternary Aurora-A/DBS1/TPX2 model supports simultaneous binding (ipTM 0.81/0.96). Design-to-hit ratio unusually good (17 designs, 13 with measurable inhibition, sub-nM hit) argues motif-scaffolding from natural weak binder is lower-variance than de novo. Third, Hao/Tomic/Przytycki (Boston University Bioinformatics + NEIDL + Chobanian & Avedisian SOM, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.07.08.737303): interpretable ML for shared and vaccine-specific immune architectures. Harmonized ISDR/HIPC dataset, 1,032 participants with matched pre/post-vax transcriptomics + ~day-28 antibody titers across influenza (n=776), HepB (n=160), and yellow fever (n=96). Independent random-forest classifiers per pathogen. Blood Transcriptional Module aggregation dominates raw gene-level features: AUC lifts 0.56→0.78 (HepB), 0.54→0.70 (influenza), 0.56→0.81 (YF). Permutation feature-importance: HepB driven by Th2 differentiation, integrin leukocyte migration, pDCs, M1 macrophages, B-cell modules; influenza by CD4+ T, M2 macrophage, c-MYC + mitotic cell cycle; yellow fever by BCR signaling, B-cell development, CORO1A-DEF6, MAIT, NK. Surrogate decision trees extract if-then rules with numerical thresholds. Cross-pathogen concordance identifies 4 shared transcriptional modules. Age but not sex residualization applied. Predicts peak (day-28) titer despite paper's framing; four shared modules are consistently-predictive-across-independent-models rather than jointly-modeled. Operational take for antibody engineers: BTM signatures identified are candidate stratification biomarkers for enriching high-responder repertoires in downstream discovery.
